SKILL.md with YAML front-matter and sections for scope, communication, work style, follow-up handling, validation, commits and short sanitized interaction examples; task-independent; rules kept only if supported by >= 2 developer turns from different sessions. Evaluation: skill injected in prompt before the original first-turn request -> agent works in isolated worktree -> LLM developer simulator issues follow-ups or 'No further requests' (max 6 turns) -> LLM judge scores

Automatic: Codex CLI replay logs; LLM judge for task completion and for simulator-vs-real follow-up matching; two-sided paired t-tests over five seed means. Manual: two annotators for skill claims (Pearson r = 0.565)

Agent = Codex CLI for all; 42 test sessions x 5 seeds = 210 replays; <= 6 turns. Criterion: mean LLM-judge score 0-100 (SD over seeds), follow-up rate, win/tie/loss vs A (Tables 1, 2, 5). Verdict rule (extractor's): quality works >= 70, partly 60-70, does not work < 60 (in line with the judge rubric, where 60-69 is 'partial success', p. 18). Cost measured only for the four Sol-low/Sol-low conditions (Table 6, agent tokens and execution time per replay), each judged on its own values; not measured for the other configurations.

rev.why: (B) + Sol-high was rated 'Partly / does not work (lower than A)': at 66.71 it is Partly under the draft's own rule, and §6 says each configuration is judged on its own, not against the others. All numbers checked against Tables 1, 2, 5, 6. Still for the author: the 70/60 thresholds are the draft's own, and the cost verdicts ('does not work (more tokens/time)') are relative to A, which the on-its-own rule does not clearly allow.

Round 1 kept cost verdicts relative to A ('does not work (more tokens/time)' for B and D, 'partly' for C, none for A), which §6 rules out: each configuration is judged on its own. Cost now judged on each condition's own Table 6 values (about 0.44-0.64M agent tokens and 92-106 s per replay): 'works' is the extractor's judgement, no threshold set by the authors; 'not measured' added for configurations without cost data. All scores re-checked against Tables 1, 2, 5 and 6; C's win/tie/loss and time added from Tables 2 and 6.

fields.v: Tasks: 42 held-out real developer sessions per split (13 developers), random 80/20 split, 5 seeds. Configurations: 2 skill generators x 4 executors x {A, B}; plus A-D on Sol-low/Sol-low and ablations E, F. Baseline: no skill. Held constant: repository commit (isolated worktree), first-turn request, task summary, simulator, scorer, prompts, replay settings, turn limit 6. Acceptance tests: none executable; LLM judge with 100-point SWE-chat rubric. Repetitions: 5 seeds of the data split. Human intervention: none (LLM simulator)

Personalized skill beats no skill in 6 of 8 generator-executor pairs, but only one significant (Sol-max with Sol-low skills, +1.82, p = .031); differences range -1.88 to +3.27. On Sol-low/Sol-low: generic skill best (68.38, +3.11, p = .003); personalized +2.37 (n.s., p = .084); random-developer skill 67.75 similar to personalized (B vs C p = .838; D vs B p = .392). Skills raise follow-up rate (24.76% -> 30.95% personalized, 30.00% generic), tokens (+35% personalized, +46% generic) and time. Personalized skill helps when >= 6 relevant evolution sessions (B-A +10.17, B-C +8.92, B-D +5.67), not otherwise. Refinement adds little over bootstrap (67.64 vs 67.49, p = .886)

Distinguished generic skill from no skill; did not reliably distinguish personalized vs other conditions (most differences n.s., large SD). Repeatability: 5 seeds with paired t-tests over seed means. Simulator validated: 89.47% of follow-ups at least partially match real developer messages. Limitations stated: small filtered sample, simulator may not reproduce humans, LLM-based scoring biases, no executable tests, reconstructed repos may lack dependencies

Small, highly filtered SWE-chat subset (206 sessions, 13 developers) may bias towards particular developers, repos and task types; limited per-developer history; LLM simulator approximates collaboration, follow-up rate is not real efficiency; task summarization, skill generation and LLM scoring may add model-dependent biases; LLM evaluation cannot replace tests or humans; random (not chronological) split assumes static preferences; only prompt-injected natural-language skills. Future: longer traces, other skill-integration methods, retrieval of task-relevant guidance combined with developer preferences

No data/code link stated in the paper; prompts given in Appendix F. No pre-registration. Programming languages not stated. Inconsistencies: Appendix C says personalized skills raise the score from 65.02 to 65.99, while Table 2 gives 65.27 -> 67.64; the first paragraph of Section 3.3 is duplicated; 'Appendix 4.2' cited for annotation details (should be Appendix B). The no-skill baseline differs between generator blocks in Table 1 (e.g., Sol-low 65.27 vs 63.26), not explained. Model names (GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra) as given. Tables 1, 2 and 6 extracted with columns split; values rebuilt by order. LaTeX residue in Fig. 2 text. Abstract states that 'task-specific skills are the most effective', whereas the results (Table 2, Section 5) find the generic skill pooled across developers best; no task-specific skill condition was run

rev.why: Missing inconsistency: the abstract (p. 1) says task-specific skills are the most effective, but the study ran no task-specific skill and found the generic skill best.
